subject: Need help with improving speed performance

messages.author: a997b66afa263bd1
messages.subject: Need help with improving speed performance
parts:
Hi everyone

I am runninng the attached codes with rstan , but it's taking a LOT of time. Just running it on a sample of 1000 observations including 5 groups take 3.17 hours (my original daaset contains ~50k obs and has 514 groups, and takes many days to run) . Can someone run it in their systems and tell me if it takes the same amount of time? How can I improve the speed?

Any help would be appreciated!

Thanks and regards
UD

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Need help with improving speed performance
parts:
Hi, here are a few tips:

- Make your Stan program a separate stand-alone .stan file, don’t put it as a character string in your R script.  This won’t speed up your model but it should help your workflow.

- normal(,100) priors on beta don’t look good to me.  Try something more stable such as normal(,1), assuming x and y have been roughly put on unit scale

- change to a ~ normal(0,1); and then in the expression for y_hat, replace “a[streetlist[n]]” by “sigma_a*a[streetlist[n]]”.  This is the so-called non-centered parameterization.

Good luck!
A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Need help with improving speed performance
parts:
You should replace the long-form arithmetic expression with a dot
product. Otherwise, besides tightening up the priors to be more
informative, I don't see much else to do. You could do some more
vectorization, but it's unlikely to help.

Are your predictors standardized?

You also have a model that's only weakly identified by priors:
because of this term

a[streetlist[n]] + beta[streetlist[n]][1] + ...

You could move to a centered parameterization if you have lots of
data, removing the a[streetlist[n]] term from y_hat sum and
instead putting it into the prior for beta[j].

beta[j] ~ normal(a[j] + u[j] * gamma, 100);

That 100 may be bad news if you don't expect beta to be on that
scale.

- Bob
